correctness.rationale: Below exponent \(p\), the p-adic valuation drops by one per derivative until zero; above exponent \(p\), the persistent factor \(p^p\) forces strict growth, while \(p^p\) itself is fixed. Thus only \(e<r\) remains. Explicit first iterates plus \(D(n)\le n\log_2n/2\) eliminate \(e=2\) for \(r=3\) and \(e=2,3\) for \(r=4\), with the finite small-prime ranges checked exactly. I independently reran all primes below 500 and exponents through 12 with no exception.

evidence: The general theorems leave \(e=2\) and \(e=3\) boundary cases at these periods.
broader_coverage.reasoning: The audited size estimates close those remaining cases.

evidence: It only forces a period to exceed the current exponent below \(p\); it does not exclude period three at exponent two or period four at exponents two and three.
The foundational source poses no-nontrivial-periodicity as a conjecture rather than proving the r=3,4 prime-power case.

Their results reduce but do not eliminate the final small prime-power exponents for periods three and four. No checked later source closes this exact branch.

value.rationale: This completely resolves the prime-power branch at the first two iterate orders beyond the period-two discussion in a longstanding arithmetic-derivative dynamics problem.

final_claim: For every prime \(p\), exponent \(e\ge1\), and \(r\in\{3,4\}\), \(D^r(p^e)=p^e\) holds exactly when \(e=p\); thus no nontrivial exact 3- or 4-cycle contains a prime power.
limitations: No statement for iterate orders above four or arbitrary composites.
